name: DS1302Z+T&R
title: DS1302: serial real-time clock and calendar with 31 bytes of RAM and a trickle charger
summary: The DS1302 keeps seconds, minutes, hours, day of week, date, month and year in BCD, in 12- or 24-hour form, with month lengths and leap years handled through 2100, and holds 31 bytes of static RAM. A host reaches it over three lines (RST, SCLK and I/O), singly or in bursts of consecutive bytes. It has two supply pins: a main supply on VCC2 and a backup cell on VCC1, which a programmable trickle charger can charge from VCC2. It runs from 2.0 V to 5.5 V, keeps time on under 300 nA at 2.0 V, and keeps time from an external 32.768 kHz crystal.
key_figures: DC to 2.0 MHz at 5V, 0.5 MHz at 2.0V

notes: An N in the part number marks the industrial range, -40°C to +85°C; the others are 0°C to 70°C.

circuits.title: Typical operating circuit
circuits.description: A microcontroller drives the three interface lines RST, SCLK and I/O straight onto the DS1302. The system supply feeds VCC2 and the microcontroller, a 32.768 kHz crystal sits across X1 and X2, and a backup cell from VCC1 to ground keeps the clock running when the supply is gone.

equations.name: Maximum trickle charge current

where.VD: drop across the selected trickle charge diode path; the trickle charge diode drop VTD is 0.7 V typical
where.R: resistor selected by RS: R1 2 kΩ, R2 4 kΩ or R3 8 kΩ

equations.note: Worked case: 5 V on VCC2, one diode and R1 give (5.0 V - 0.7 V) / 2 kΩ ≈ 2.2 mA. The current falls as the supercapacitor on VCC1 charges and the difference between VCC2 and VCC1 shrinks.

operation.text: The chip draws from whichever supply pin is higher. VCC2 takes over once it is more than 0.2 V above VCC1; below VCC1, VCC1 runs the chip. VCC1 alone also serves a single-supply or battery-only design, with time and RAM held on less than 1 µW.
X1 and X2 take a standard 32.768 kHz quartz crystal specified for a 6 pF load. In place of a crystal, an external 32.768 kHz oscillator may drive X1 with X2 left open.

Timekeeping error comes from the crystal's own tolerance, from any mismatch between the oscillator's load capacitance and the load the crystal was cut for, and from the crystal's drift with temperature. Outside noise picked up by the oscillator tends to make the clock gain time.
The crystal sits right beside X1 and X2. A local ground plane on layer 2 lies under the crystal and its two pads, and a ground-connected guard ring surrounds the X1 and X2 traces.

Every transfer opens with a command byte sent LSB first. Bit 0 picks write (0) or read (1), bits 1 to 5 give the register address, bit 6 picks clock/calendar (0) or RAM (1), and bit 7 must be 1, or writes are blocked.

Driving RST high starts the control logic and opens the shift register to a command; pulling it low ends any single-byte or burst transfer and puts I/O into high impedance. SCLK must already be low when RST goes high. At power-up RST must be kept low until VCC exceeds 2.0 V. Each SCLK cycle runs falling edge first, then rising edge: input bits are sampled on rising edges and output bits change on falling edges.
After the eight clocks of a write command, the next eight rising edges take in one data byte, bit 0 first. Extra clocks after that byte do nothing.

After the eight clocks of a read command, data bit 0 comes out on the very next falling edge and the rest follow on the next seven. I/O goes to high impedance on each rising edge. While RST stays high, more clocks send further bytes, which allows continuous burst reads.

Address 31 (bits 1 to 5 all 1) selects burst mode, for clock or RAM by bit 6 and for read or write by bit 0. A burst starts at bit 0 of address 0. A clock burst write must fill all of the first eight registers, control register included, or nothing is taken; a RAM burst write stores each byte as it arrives, with no need to send all 31. Clock addresses 9 to 31 and RAM address 31 hold no data. The trickle charge register cannot be reached by burst.
When a clock burst read begins, the chip copies the time into a shadow register set, and the burst returns that copy while counting goes on, so a rollover during the read cannot tear the result.
Seven read/write registers hold seconds, minutes, hours, date, month, day of week and year, all in BCD.
CH sits in bit 7 of the seconds register. Writing 1 stops the oscillator and drops the chip into standby below 100 nA; writing 0 starts the clock. Its state at first power-up is undefined.
Setting bit 7 of the hours byte to 1 selects 12-hour time, where bit 5 flags PM when 1. With bit 7 at 0 (24-hour time), bit 5 instead counts the twenties, for hours 20 to 23.

WP sits in bit 7 of the control register; bits 0 to 6 always read 0. With WP at 1, writes to every other register are refused, and a clock burst write with WP set moves no data. WP is undefined at power-up, so it is cleared before the first write.

The charger links VCC2 to VCC1 through a switch, one or two series diodes and one of three resistors. Bits 7 to 4 (TCS) must hold 1010 to enable it; anything else disables it, which guards against turning it on by accident. Bits 3 to 2 (DS) pick one diode (01) or two (10), and bits 1 to 0 (RS) pick 2 kΩ, 4 kΩ or 8 kΩ; DS of 00 or 11, or RS of 00, also leaves it off. It is off at power-up. The diode and resistor are chosen for the largest charging current wanted for a battery or supercapacitor.
The 31 bytes of static RAM occupy consecutive addresses in the RAM space and keep their contents on the backup supply. A RAM burst reads or writes them in order from address 0.
The DS1302 follows on from the DS1202 and works with it, adding the second supply pin, the trickle charger on VCC1 and seven more bytes of scratchpad RAM.
